May. Mihai wants to climb Omu Peak in the Bucegi mountains with Ana and Andrei. Ana is very cautious. They’re packing their rucksacks in the living room.
We leave at six, provided nobody oversleeps.
I’m in, as long as we stop so I can draw at the summit.
And what if it rains? The forecast says there might be a storm in the afternoon.
If it rains, we’ll stay at the mountain hut. It has beds and a stove.
OK. But I’m packing the rain capes just in case. And a torch. And a blanket.
Miss, at this rate the rucksack will weigh more than I do.
Better too much than too little. And Rosa Elena? Are you sure your mother can look after her?
Yes. Unless the baby gets a temperature, my mother is happy to stay with her.
If I’d known earlier, I’d have bought some new boots. Mine are ten years old.
I’ll give you my mother’s, provided you don’t tell her you broke them.
And what if we get lost?
We won’t get lost, unless someone starts drawing butterflies and wanders off the path.
Ha-ha. OK, OK. I promise not to draw butterflies… unless they’re really beautiful.
por-see-a-KA-so: run together, like a single word. Spaniards use it constantly.
A proverb with repeated “que”: meh-HOR-keh-SO-breh / keh-keh-FAL-teh. It sounds funny, but it’s very common!
You’ve learned “si” (chapter 42). Spanish has several more conjunctions of condition, with different shades. ALL of them take the SUBJUNCTIVE:
En caso de que llueva, nos quedamos.
Puedes venir, siempre que no te quejes.
Haría todo con tal de que fuera feliz.
Se queda, a no ser que tenga fiebre.
Unlike “si”, these conjunctions DON’T go with the indicative: “en caso de que llueve” is wrong. Correct: en caso de que llueva.
“Siempre que” + INDICATIVE means “whenever”: Siempre que viene, trae flores. + SUBJUNCTIVE = “provided that”: Siempre que vengas, te espero.
2. Negative conditions: a menos que, a no ser que
These two expressions mean “unless”. Careful: the verb that follows is AFFIRMATIVE!
Te llamo si no estoy ocupado.
Te llamo a no ser que esté ocupado.
The typical mistake: “a menos que no llueva”. DON’T double the negative! “A menos que” already contains the idea of “not”, just like English “unless”.
An elegant structure, especially in speech: DE + infinitive replaces a clause with “si”:
Si lo sé, te lo digo.
Si lo hubiera sabido, habría venido.
“De haberlo sabido” (had I known) is the most common expression in this family. It’s worth learning by heart.
“Por si” shows you’re doing something to be ready for a possibility, like English “in case”. Surprisingly, it’s followed by the INDICATIVE:
I’m taking the umbrella in case it rains.
I’ll give you my number in case you need anything.
I’m packing a blanket, just in case.
Useful proverbs: Más vale prevenir que curar (Prevention is better than cure). Mejor que sobre que que falte (Better too much than too little).
Vamos a menos que no llueva.
Lleva una manta, por si acaso.
Lleva una manta, en caso de.
Lleva una manta, a menos que.

They set off at a quarter to six, because Ana hadn’t been able to sleep and had woken everyone at five. The sky was clear, such an intense blue that it looked painted. Mihai said it was a good sign. Ana said good signs don’t exist, only weather forecasts.
The path began in a fir forest, next to a fast-flowing river. Andrei stopped every ten minutes to draw something: a red mushroom, a heart-shaped stone, an abandoned cabin.
“At this rate we’ll reach the summit in September,” Mihai protested, although he was smiling.
“You promised we’d stop so I could draw,” Andrei answered. “As long as I get to draw, you can walk as fast as you like.”
At midday they came out of the forest. The landscape changed suddenly: there were no more trees, just short grass, grey rocks and, in the distance, Omu Peak with the little stone hut at the top.

They sat down to eat on a flat rock. Ana took out of her rucksack sandwiches, fruit, chocolate, dried fruit, flasks of tea, a first-aid kit, two torches, three rain capes and a blanket. Andrei stared at her wide-eyed.
“Miss, you’ve been carrying all that since six?”
“Just in case,” Ana answered, and gave him a piece of chocolate.

That was when Mihai saw the clouds. They were coming from the west, dark and fast, like an army. Within minutes they had covered the sun. The wind began to blow hard, and the temperature dropped suddenly.
“We have to hurry,” said Mihai, packing up. “The hut is an hour away. If we stay here, the storm will catch us out in the open.”
“And what if we go back down?” asked Andrei, rather pale.
“Going down takes longer. Unless we find another hut, the one at the top is the only option.”

They started climbing fast. After twenty minutes the first drops fell. After thirty, the rain turned to hail. Ana handed out the rain capes without saying a word. Nobody laughed at her rucksack any more.
The fog came suddenly. One moment you could see the summit; the next, you couldn’t see anything more than five metres away. The path markings, painted red on the rocks, disappeared in the fog.
“Don’t get separated from me!” Mihai shouted over the wind. “Andrei, hold on to Ana’s rucksack. Ana, hold on to mine.”
They walked like that, in single file, for what felt like forever. A clap of thunder rang out so close that Andrei threw himself to the ground. Ana pulled him up and they kept going.
Then Mihai stopped. He had lost the red markings. He looked right, then left. There was nothing but fog and wet rocks. For the first time all day, Ana saw fear on his face.

It was Andrei who saved them. He remembered something: when he had stopped to draw the abandoned cabin, he had also copied the map on the door. He had it in his sketchbook, protected in plastic in the inside pocket of his jacket.

They took it out carefully, shielding it from the rain with their hands. In the drawing, with an architect’s precision, you could see the path, a spring and a big rock shaped like a man’s head: the Babele.
“If the spring is here,” said Andrei, pointing, “and we can hear water on the left… the path must be on the right.”
They listened. Through the howling of the wind, they could faintly hear the murmur of water.
Ten minutes later they found a red marking. Half an hour later, soaked to the skin, shivering and with aching legs, they reached the hut.

The warden, a huge man with a white beard, opened the door and let them in without asking any questions. Inside it smelled of firewood and soup. There was a lit stove and six or seven climbers drying their clothes.
Ana took the blanket out of her rucksack and put it round Andrei’s shoulders. Then she took out the flask of tea, which was still hot, and shared it with everyone.
Mihai didn’t say anything for a long time. Finally, when they were dry and had a bowl of soup in front of them, he looked at Ana.
“I’ll never laugh at your rucksack again. Never. I promise.”

The storm lasted all night. They slept in bunk beds, squeezed together, listening to the wind battering the stone walls. Andrei couldn’t sleep. He took out his sketchbook and, by the light of Ana’s torch, drew the inside of the hut: the stove, the climbers, the soup, the blanket.
The next morning, the sky was clear again, as if nothing had happened. From the summit you could see the mountains all the way to the horizon, covered with a thin layer of hail glittering in the sun.
Andrei drew the view for an hour, as promised. Mihai and Ana sat down next to him, in silence, with tea in their hands.
“Had I known,” Ana said suddenly, “I wouldn’t have come.”
Mihai looked at her, worried. She smiled.
“And I’d have missed this,” she added, pointing at the mountains. “So I’m glad I didn’t know.”
When they got down to the village, Mihai called his mother. Elena answered on the first ring, her voice shaking: she had seen the news about the storm and hadn’t slept all night.
“We’re fine, Mum. All of us. Thanks to Ana’s rucksack… and Andrei’s sketchbook.”
At the other end of the line a little voice could be heard: “Daddy! Bu… bunicu!” It was Rosa Elena, who had just learned to say “bunicu” (Grandpa) and called everyone that, even Mihai.
Mihai laughed, for the first time since the storm. “Yes, sweetheart. Daddy’s coming now. Unless your mother decides to pack another blanket, we’ll be home for dinner.”
A week later, Ana received a parcel at home. There was no sender. Inside was a pair of new hiking boots, exactly her size, and a note in the clumsy writing of someone not used to writing in Spanish.
“For the lady with the rucksack. In case she comes back to the mountains, let her have good boots. The warden of Omu.”

Ana looked at the note for a long time. She didn’t understand how the warden had found out her address. Until Mihai confessed that he had left him his hospital business card, in case he ever needed a doctor up there.
For his part, Andrei took the drawing of the hut to the Fine Arts school. His teacher looked at it for a long time and asked him how he had managed to draw so much light in such a dark place.
“With my teacher’s torch,” Andrei answered. “She always has two, just in case.”

The teacher didn’t understand the answer, but he put the drawing up on the wall of the main corridor. Underneath, Andrei wrote the title in Romanian and Spanish: “Refuge. Until the storm comes, nobody knows what it’s worth.”
And that evening, when Ana put the rucksack away in the cupboard, she didn’t empty it completely. She left a torch, a blanket and a bar of chocolate inside. Just in case.
Mihai saw her from the doorway, but this time he didn’t say anything. He just smiled and, without her noticing, added an empty flask, ready for the next cup of tea.
